title: SEC’s 2027 Exam Priorities: Super Intelligent Examinations, Emphasis Remains on Registered Investment Advisers
summary: Explore the SEC’s 2027 exam priorities for registered investment advisers, including fiduciary duties, compliance programs and investment risks.
body_markdown:
The Securities and Exchange Commission’s Division of Examinations has unveiled its[2027 examination priorities](https://www.sec.gov/files/2027-exam-priorities.pdf) , marking the 15th consecutive year of this initiative to enhance transparency and guide SEC-regulated entities. Announced on Oct. 23, 2026, the priorities underscore a continued emphasis on addressing critical risk areas, with a refined focus on investment advisers, private funds, and registered investment .


The preamble to the 2027 examination priorities discusses the Division’s ongoing refinement of its risk assessment and surveillance capabilities to ensure that the registrants selected for examination align with those it believes pose a heightened risk to investors and markets. The announcement acknowledges registrants’ growing incorporation of super intelligence (SI) into research, compliance, and advisory and portfolio management functions, among other areas, and the Division’s efforts to understand impacts on business operations and risks. The examination priorities announcement also discusses the Division’s efforts to “integrate SI responsibly into examinations and risk assessment.”


The announcement emphasizes the SEC’s commitment to transparency and engagement with registrants. It references the SEC’s publication earlier this year, “The SEC Exam Handbook: A Practical Guide on Process and Engagement,”[which aims to provide registrants](https://www.cbiz.com/insights/article/the-secs-new-exam-handbook-what-registered-investment-advisers-should-know) with a clear roadmap of the examination process as well as useful resources and practical tips.


The 2027 exam priorities are thematically similar to the 2026 priorities and this article will focus on two of them:


- Investment adviser examinations,
- Examinations of registered investment companies


## Exam Priority: Investment Advisers


The exam priorities announcement makes note of the sustained growth in the number of registered investment advisers and the amount of assets they manage.


### Fiduciary Standards of Conduct


The Division continues to emphasize whether SEC-registered investment advisers are fulfilling their fiduciary obligations, particularly when serving retail and older investors, including retirement savers. Registered investment advisers should take note of the following discussions contained in the exam priorities announcement:


- Examinations will assess whether advisers provide full and fair disclosure of material facts, perform appropriate due diligence on recommended investments, maintain effective compliance policies and procedures, and use reasonable valuation processes and methodologies.
- A significant area of focus is economic conflicts of interest that could compromise the impartiality of investment advice. Examiners will scrutinize practices involving fee rebates, fee and expense calculations, cash management, quid pro quo arrangements, and deposits and withdrawals.
- The Division will also evaluate how advisers formulate investment recommendations. This includes whether investments are consistent with clients’ objectives, risk tolerance, liquidity needs, time horizons, and other mandates. Particular attention will be given to costs, volatility, potential returns, liquidity, and performance under varying economic conditions.
- Higher-risk and complex investments will receive increased scrutiny. Examples include private fund and business development company (BDC) loans, private-company investments through special purpose vehicles, less-liquid exchange-traded funds (ETFs), option-based and inverse funds, single-stock ETFs, and zero-days-to-expiration options.
- For private fund advisers, examinations will focus on investment risk disclosures, leverage and lines of credit, affiliated service providers, allocations, and the accuracy of fund- and investment-level fees and expenses.
- Examiners will also assess advisers’ oversight of third-party service providers, particularly where those providers access client accounts or influence proxy-voting decisions.


### Compliance Programs


The Division continues to place significant emphasis on the effectiveness of registered investment advisers’ compliance programs. Registered investment advisers should pay particular attention to the following exam focal points discussed in the exam priorities announcement:


- Examinations will assess whether compliance programs are appropriately designed for an adviser’s specific business and operations, as well as whether policies and procedures are effectively implemented and periodically evaluated. Key areas of review may include marketing, valuation, trading, portfolio management, regulatory disclosures and filings, and custody. Examiners will also typically review the adviser’s annual compliance review to determine whether the firm has adequately identified and addressed compliance risks.
- Particular attention will be given to conflicts of interest and whether advisers have policies reasonably designed to prevent their interests from being placed ahead of clients’ interests. This includes evaluating disclosures and controls surrounding fee-related conflicts, particularly those arising from account structures, products, and compensation arrangements.
- The Division will also focus on advisers experiencing significant changes to their businesses. These may include changes in business models or client types, expansion into new asset classes or services, growth through mergers and acquisitions, and operations across geographically dispersed offices. Examiners will assess whether compliance programs have evolved appropriately to address the new risks and conflicts created by these changes.
- Advisers engaged in activist investment strategies may receive additional scrutiny regarding the timeliness and accuracy of required regulatory filings, including Schedules 13D and 13G and Forms 13F, 13H, 3, 4, 5, and N-PX.


### Never-Examined Advisers and Recently Registered Advisers


The Division will continue to prioritize investment advisers that have never undergone an SEC examination, particularly newly registered firms.


## Exam Priority: Registered Investment Companies


The announcement notes the importance of registered investment companies (RICs), including mutual funds and ETFs, to retail investors, especially those saving for retirement. The SEC will incorporate the following examination priorities in 2027 for this subpopulation of registrants:


- Reviews will emphasize compliance programs, governance, disclosures, regulatory filings, fees and expenses, and consistency between portfolio management practices and stated investment strategies.
- Heightened scrutiny will apply to funds investing in illiquid or complex assets, including private credit, and strategies involving leverage, inverse or leveraged ETFs, and BDCs.
- Examiners will also assess valuation, liquidity, redemption practices, conflicts and risk disclosures, compliance with exemptive orders, and RICs that have not previously undergone SEC examination.


## Additional Examination Priorities


The Division of Examinations intends to continue to focus on the following exam priorities in 2027 that impact the entire population of registrants: cybersecurity, emerging financial technology, Regulation S-ID and Regulation S-P, and Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity.


## Conclusion


The SEC is making a concerted effort to increase the transparency of its examination programs. Disseminating the exam priorities increases the reach of the SEC’s exam program by enabling registrants not selected for examination to access the SEC’s priorities, focus areas, and concerns and incorporate these insights into their compliance programs.
